title: Why Google Scrapped Brainteaser Interviews (2013)
explainer: For decades, elite tech companies tested candidates with puzzles like 'how many golf balls fit in an airplane.' In 2013, Google's own head of People Operations, Laszlo Bock, told the New York Times the company's internal data showed these brainteasers 'don't predict anything' about job performance and mostly just made the interviewer feel smart. Google shifted toward structured behavioral interviews with a consistent scoring rubric instead - a reminder that the format of a technical interview is itself a historically contingent, evidence-tested design choice, not a fixed obstacle you have to out-trick.

title: The Yerkes-Dodson Law and Interview-Day Nerves (1908)
explainer: In 1908, psychologists Robert Yerkes and John Dodson ran experiments showing that performance improves with arousal only up to a point, after which added stress makes performance worse - a relationship usually drawn as an inverted U. The effect has since been widely observed in humans under evaluative pressure, including tasks much like a technical interview: a little nervous energy sharpens focus, but too much tips into the kind of overload that makes you blank on material you actually know. It's a useful frame for why repeated practice under mild, realistic pressure beats either no rehearsal or panic-inducing last-minute cramming.
